title: Design an Ad Serving System
brief: A publisher network needs a service that picks one ad for every page view in well under a tenth of a second. Each pick must respect advertiser targeting and budgets, and every impression and click has to be recorded for billing without slowing the page down.
constraints: Return an ad within 80 ms at p99
Peak of 60,000 ad requests per second (1.2M visitors, about one request every 20 seconds each)
Choose ads using the visitor's context: location, device, page topic
Never lose an impression or click event, but never block the ad response on recording it
Let the ranking logic be rolled out to a slice of traffic first (A/B test)

scenarios.title: Typical peak hour
scenarios.description: The expected 60K requests per second arrive steadily.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Walk through one ad request from the page to the response. Which hops are on the critical path and which can be moved off it?
scenarios.debrief: The ad server does cached lookups and calls ranking; event recording happens off the request path.

scenarios.title: Big event traffic (2x)
scenarios.description: A major live event doubles the request rate within minutes.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Which component saturates first when traffic doubles, and how would you scale it without re-architecting?
scenarios.debrief: Autoscaling widens the ad server, ranking and workers, and the queue's partitions take the doubled event rate.

scenarios.title: Ranking model slows down
scenarios.description: The component that scores and ranks candidate ads becomes 6x slower.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: The ranking step is suddenly slow. What does the visitor see, and how does your design protect the 80 ms budget?
scenarios.debrief: The breaker cuts ranking off at its timeout and a simpler rule picks the ad, so the 80 ms budget holds.

scenarios.title: Campaign cache is lost
scenarios.description: The hot campaign data store disappears and every lookup falls through to the database.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: With the cache gone, what absorbs the read load? Would you rather serve stale campaigns or fail?
scenarios.debrief: Three cache replicas mean losing one reduces capacity, and the database with read replicas covers the extra misses.

scenarios.title: Event pipeline outage
scenarios.description: The queue that carries impression and click events goes offline.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Events cannot be queued. Do ads keep serving? Where are events held until the pipeline returns?
scenarios.debrief: Spare queue partitions keep accepting events, and the ad response never waited on them.

requirements.text: Ads are returned within the latency budget at peak load
At least 99% of requests are served during the 2x spike
Impression and click events are recorded asynchronously (queue plus consumer)
A slow ranking model cannot push responses past the latency target
Event recording is decoupled from the ad response with an async link
The design explains how ranking changes can be tested on part of the traffic

rubric: The ad response path avoids the primary database on every request (cache, in-memory index, or precomputed candidates).
Impression and click logging goes through a queue so it cannot slow or fail the response.
Budget and pacing are handled without a synchronous global lock on the hot path.
A slow ranking step has a timeout and a cheaper fallback.
Components on the hot path run as multiple instances behind a balancer.
Ranking runs apart from the core ad pick, or is called behind a timeout, so a slow model degrades quality instead of availability.

capabilities.label: Pick an ad
capabilities.hint: Filter campaigns by targeting and choose the best bid for this page view

capabilities.label: Rank with the model
capabilities.hint: Score candidate ads with the relevance model for 70% of requests. Without it a simpler rule picks the ad.

capabilities.label: Record impressions and clicks
capabilities.hint: Persist billing events. Belongs off the request path.

reference.summary: Pick ads from cached campaigns, keep the ranking model behind a breaker, and record events asynchronously.
design: User, then a Load Balancer (3 instances), then an Ad Server (56 replicas, autoscale to 130, circuit breaker, 50 ms timeout) running 'Pick an ad'.
It reads a Cache (3 replicas, 97% hit, request coalescing) in front of a Database with 2 read replicas.
Ranking runs in a separate Service (40 replicas, autoscale) behind the breaker.
Impressions and clicks go to a Queue (8 partitions) asynchronously, read by Workers (batch 40, idempotent, autoscale).
tradeoffs: Ranking as its own service costs about $5K more a month than running it inside the ad server, but a slow model degrades quality, not availability.
Autoscaling pays for spike capacity only part of the time.
